passage.title: Clinical Vignette: Chronic Kidney Disease
passage.text: A 68-year-old woman with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents for follow-up. She reports progressive fatigue, decreased urine output, and bilateral leg swelling over the past month. Medications include lisinopril, metformin, and amlodipine. Blood pressure is 158/96 mmHg; she has 2+ pitting edema to the knees. Laboratory values are shown in Table 1. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein. Renal ultrasound reveals bilaterally small, echogenic kidneys.

stem: A nephrologist adds a loop diuretic. Which mechanism of action makes furosemide effective for this patient's edema?

choices.text: hyperkalemia is caused by ACE inhibitor use alone, independent of any reduction in GFR
hyperkalemia results from decreased filtered potassium load, preventing renal potassium excretion
elevated potassium results from transcellular shifts caused by metabolic alkalosis shifting K⁺ into cells
reduced GFR from chronic diabetic nephropathy impairs potassium secretion in the cortical collecting duct, leading to hyperkalemia

explanation.short: In CKD, fewer functional nephrons means reduced aldosterone-responsive collecting duct capacity for K⁺ secretion. Concurrent metabolic acidosis (from impaired H⁺ excretion) shifts K⁺ out of cells, further raising plasma levels.
explanation.detailed: In CKD, fewer functional nephrons means reduced aldosterone-responsive collecting duct capacity for K⁺ secretion. Concurrent metabolic acidosis (from impaired H⁺ excretion) shifts K⁺ out of cells, further raising plasma levels. This item tests integration of clinical findings with underlying physiology.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: reduced GFR from chronic diabetic nephropathy impairs potassium secretion in the cortical collecting duct, leading to hyperkalemia.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: While ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone-mediated K⁺ secretion, the primary driver here is CKD reducing functional nephron mass and tubular secretory capacity overall
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Potassium excretion is driven primarily by secretion in the collecting duct, not filtered load; GFR reduction impairs secretory capacity in remaining nephrons
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This patient has metabolic acidosis (HCO₃⁻ 14 mEq/L), which shifts K⁺ out of cells (raising plasma K⁺); alkalosis would shift it in; the primary cause is reduced tubular secretion
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: reduced GFR from chronic diabetic nephropathy impairs potassium secretion in the cortical collecting duct, leading to hyperkalemia
explanation.common_trap: Focusing on individual lab values rather than the clinical pattern as a whole.
explanation.how_to_think: Identify the primary disturbance from the lab pattern, then trace the underlying mechanism.

passage.title: Electrochemistry Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a prospective randomized clinical trial to investigate electrochemistry. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: A galvanic cell uses zinc and copper half-cells. Which statement correctly identifies the anode?

choices.text: the anode is whichever electrode has the higher concentration of metal ions
the zinc electrode is the anode because zinc is oxidized (loses electrons), which drives the spontaneous cell
the copper electrode is the anode because copper has a higher reduction potential and accepts electrons
in a galvanic cell the anode is the positive terminal, so it is where reduction occurs

explanation.short: Oxidation at the Anode (An Ox), Reduction at the Cathode (Red Cat). In a galvanic cell, the more easily oxidized metal becomes the anode. Zinc (E° = −0.76 V) is more easily oxidized than copper (E° = +0.34 V).
explanation.detailed: Oxidation at the Anode (An Ox), Reduction at the Cathode (Red Cat). In a galvanic cell, the more easily oxidized metal becomes the anode. Zinc (E° = −0.76 V) is more easily oxidized than copper (E° = +0.34 V). This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: the zinc electrode is the anode because zinc is oxidized (loses electrons), which drives the spontaneous cell.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Electrode identity (anode/cathode) is determined by the half-reaction type (oxidation/reduction), not ion concentration
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: A higher reduction potential means copper is preferentially reduced at the cathode, not oxidized at the anode
wrong_answer_explanations.D: In a galvanic cell the anode is negative (source of electrons flowing out); reduction occurs at the cathode, not the anode

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: An Ox, Red Cat. Galvanic anode is negative; electrolytic anode is positive (connected to +).
explanation.common_trap: Students flip anode/cathode sign in galvanic vs electrolytic cells. In both, oxidation is always at the anode.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.text: Researchers used a retrospective cohort study in hospitalized patients to investigate electrochemistry. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: The Nernst equation predicts how cell potential changes as a reaction proceeds. At equilibrium, which value does Q equal?

choices.text: E > E°cell because when Q < 1 the reaction quotient term (−RT/nF × ln Q) is positive, adding to E°
E = E°cell because Q < 1 has no effect until equilibrium
E is undefined when Q departs from 1
E < E°cell because non-standard conditions always reduce the driving force

explanation.short: Nernst equation: E = E° − (RT/nF)ln Q. When Q < 1, ln Q < 0, so the subtracted term becomes negative, raising E above E°.
explanation.detailed: Nernst equation: E = E° − (RT/nF)ln Q. When Q < 1, ln Q < 0, so the subtracted term becomes negative, raising E above E°. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: A is correct: E > E°cell because when Q < 1 the reaction quotient term (−RT/nF × ln Q) is positive, adding to E°.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Q < 1 means products are low relative to reactants, increasing the driving force and raising E above E°
wrong_answer_explanations.C: The Nernst equation applies at any Q; it is well-defined for all positive Q values
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Non-standard E can be higher than E° when Q < 1; the assumption that it is always lower ignores the log term's sign

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Q < 1 → E > E°. Q > 1 → E < E°. Q = Keq → E = 0 (equilibrium).
explanation.common_trap: Students assume non-standard always means lower potential; direction depends on whether Q < 1 or Q > 1.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: A mixture of H2 (M = 2) and O2 (M = 32) effuses through a small opening. Which gas effuses faster and by what factor?

choices.text: H2 effuses twice as fast because its molar mass is half that of O2
O2 effuses faster because it has more mass and therefore more momentum
both gases effuse at the same rate because temperature determines kinetic energy equally
H2 effuses 4 times faster than O2 because rate is inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass

explanation.short: Graham's law: rate ∝ 1/√M. Rate(H2)/Rate(O2) = √(32/2) = √16 = 4.
explanation.detailed: Graham's law: rate ∝ 1/√M. Rate(H2)/Rate(O2) = √(32/2) = √16 = 4. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: H2 effuses 4 times faster than O2 because rate is inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: H2/O2 molar mass ratio is 1/16, so rate ratio = √16 = 4, not 2; square root is required
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Graham's law gives rate ∝ 1/√M; heavier gas is slower, not faster, regardless of momentum
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Temperature equalizes average kinetic energy but not speed; lighter molecules move faster at the same KE
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Graham's law: ratio of rates = square root of the inverse molar mass ratio.
explanation.common_trap: Students use the molar mass ratio directly rather than its square root.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: Red blood cells placed in a 0.9% NaCl solution maintain their normal shape. When transferred to distilled water, they swell and lyse. Which colligative property explains lysis?

choices.text: NaCl has a lower boiling point because ionic solutes disrupt hydrogen bonding more than covalent solutes
glucose has a higher boiling point because larger molecules create more surface interactions with water
both solutions have identical boiling points because molality determines boiling point elevation regardless of solute identity
NaCl solution has a higher boiling point because it dissociates into two ions (Na+ and Cl−), doubling the effective particle concentration

explanation.short: ΔTb = iKbm. NaCl (i ≈ 2) doubles the effective molality relative to glucose (i = 1), producing twice the boiling point elevation.
explanation.detailed: ΔTb = iKbm. NaCl (i ≈ 2) doubles the effective molality relative to glucose (i = 1), producing twice the boiling point elevation. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: NaCl solution has a higher boiling point because it dissociates into two ions (Na+ and Cl−), doubling the effective particle concentration.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Both ionic and covalent solutes elevate boiling point; NaCl elevates it more because it produces more particles per formula unit
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Boiling point elevation is a colligative property depending on particle number, not molecular size or polarity
wrong_answer_explanations.C: The van't Hoff factor i accounts for dissociation; NaCl has i = 2, glucose i = 1, so they differ at equal molality
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Colligative properties depend on particle count, not identity. Ionic solutes dissociate, multiplying their effect.
explanation.common_trap: Forgetting the van't Hoff factor i and treating NaCl as a non-electrolyte is the classic trap.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Nucleophilic Substitution Scenario

stem: A primary alkyl bromide reacts with sodium cyanide (strong nucleophile) in acetone. Which mechanism and stereochemical outcome are most expected?

choices.text: SN1 with racemization, because the primary substrate forms a stable primary carbocation that is attacked from both faces
No reaction because primary substrates are too stable for nucleophilic substitution
SN2 with inversion of configuration, because the primary substrate is unhindered and the strong nucleophile performs backside attack
E2 elimination because cyanide is too bulky to reach the backside

explanation.short: SN2: strong nucleophile + primary (or methyl) substrate + polar aprotic solvent → inversion. SN1: weak nucleophile or solvolysis + tertiary substrate + polar protic solvent → racemization.
explanation.detailed: SN2: strong nucleophile + primary (or methyl) substrate + polar aprotic solvent → inversion. SN1: weak nucleophile or solvolysis + tertiary substrate + polar protic solvent → racemization. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: SN2 with inversion of configuration, because the primary substrate is unhindered and the strong nucleophile performs backside attack.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Primary carbocations are highly unstable and do not form under normal conditions; SN1 requires at least secondary (preferably tertiary) substrates
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Primary substrates are among the most reactive in SN2 due to minimal steric hindrance; they do react readily
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Cyanide is a linear, compact anion and is not sterically hindered; bulky bases favor elimination but cyanide is not bulky

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: SN2: primary, strong Nu, polar aprotic, inversion. SN1: tertiary, weak Nu, polar protic, racemization.
explanation.common_trap: Students default to SN1 for any substrate; remember primary substrates cannot form stable carbocations.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Clinical Vignette: Adrenal Cortex Pathology
passage.text: A 34-year-old woman presents with a six-month history of fatigue, weight loss, nausea, and salt craving. stem: The laboratory pattern in Table 1 (low Na⁺, high K⁺, low glucose, low cortisol, high ACTH) best localizes this patient's pathology to which site?

choices.text: Cushing's syndrome with adrenal hyperplasia, which causes cortisol excess and would suppress ACTH in most primary adrenal forms

primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease): destruction of the adrenal cortex eliminates both cortisol and aldosterone, removing cortisol's negative feedback on the pituitary and causing compensatory ACTH elevation
tertiary adrenal insufficiency from hypothalamic CRH deficiency, which would reduce both ACTH and cortisol without mineralocorticoid loss
secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary failure, which would cause low ACTH and low cortisol without aldosterone deficiency or hyperpigmentation

passage.title: Nucleophilic Substitution Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a double-blind crossover design with healthy volunteers to investigate nucleophilic substitution. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: A researcher treats a secondary substrate with a weak nucleophile in a polar protic solvent at room temperature. What is the most likely mechanism?

choices.text: No reaction because elimination requires a tertiary substrate
E2 elimination product because a strong base at high temperature with a secondary substrate favors elimination over substitution
SN1 because secondary substrates always ionize to carbocations in polar solvents
SN2 substitution because methoxide is also a nucleophile and secondary substrates always substitute

explanation.short: Strong base + heat → elimination (E2). At room temperature with a good nucleophile → SN2. Secondary substrates are at the crossroads; temperature and base strength decide.
explanation.detailed: Strong base + heat → elimination (E2). At room temperature with a good nucleophile → SN2. Secondary substrates are at the crossroads; temperature and base strength decide. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: E2 elimination product because a strong base at high temperature with a secondary substrate favors elimination over substitution.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: E2 elimination occurs at primary and secondary substrates; tertiary substrates favor E1 or E2 but are not the only option
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Secondary substrates can do SN2, but the combination of strong base + heat + secondary strongly favors E2
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Methoxide is both a strong base and nucleophile; high temperature and secondary substrate tip the competition toward E2 elimination

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Heat + strong base + secondary → E2. Room temp + good nucleophile + secondary → SN2.
explanation.common_trap: Students forget that the same reagent (e.g., NaOEt) can act as nucleophile or base; context (temperature, substrate) determines which role dominates.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: An aldehyde is treated with excess sodium borohydride (NaBH4) in methanol. What is the primary product?

choices.text: an acetal, because methanol attacks the carbonyl under all conditions
a secondary alcohol, because NaBH4 always adds two carbons to the carbonyl
a carboxylic acid, because NaBH4 oxidizes aldehydes in the presence of base
a primary alcohol (from aldehyde reduction) because NaBH4 delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon

explanation.short: NaBH4 donates hydride (H−) to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon. Aldehydes (RCHO) → primary alcohols (RCH2OH). Ketones (RCOR′) → secondary alcohols (RCHOHR′).
explanation.detailed: NaBH4 donates hydride (H−) to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon. Aldehydes (RCHO) → primary alcohols (RCH2OH). Ketones (RCOR′) → secondary alcohols (RCHOHR′). This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: a primary alcohol (from aldehyde reduction) because NaBH4 delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Acetal formation requires an acid catalyst and two equivalents of alcohol; NaBH4 reduction proceeds differently
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Hydride addition replaces C=O with C–OH; no carbons are added—only hydrogen. Aldehydes give primary alcohols, ketones give secondary
wrong_answer_explanations.C: NaBH4 is a reducing agent that delivers H−; it does not oxidize and does not produce carboxylic acids
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: NaBH4/LiAlH4 reduce carbonyls. Aldehyde → 1° alcohol; ketone → 2° alcohol; ester/acid → 1° alcohol (LiAlH4 only).
explanation.common_trap: Confusing reduction product class: aldehydes give primary, ketones give secondary—not both secondary.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Stereochemistry Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a controlled murine model with genetic knockout to investigate stereochemistry. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: Two compounds share the same molecular formula and sequence of bonds but differ in the spatial arrangement of groups around one chiral center. They are non-superimposable mirror images. How are they related?

choices.text: they are identical compounds viewed from different angles
they are constitutional isomers because they differ in the spatial arrangement of atoms
they are diastereomers because having two chiral centers always creates diastereomers
they are enantiomers because they are non-superimposable mirror images differing at every chiral center

explanation.short: Enantiomers: non-superimposable mirror images. Diastereomers: stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images (differ at some but not all chiral centers). Meso compounds are achiral despite having stereocenters.
explanation.detailed: Enantiomers: non-superimposable mirror images. Diastereomers: stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images (differ at some but not all chiral centers). Meso compounds are achiral despite having stereocenters. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: they are enantiomers because they are non-superimposable mirror images differing at every chiral center.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Non-superimposability is the test for enantiomers; if the two structures were identical, one could be superimposed on the other
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Constitutional isomers differ in connectivity; stereoisomers share the same connectivity but differ in spatial arrangement
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Diastereomers differ at some but not all chiral centers; the mirror image relationship that is non-superimposable defines enantiomers
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Enantiomers = mirror images that are non-superimposable. Diastereomers = stereoisomers that are not mirror images.
explanation.common_trap: Thinking that any molecule with two stereocenters must form diastereomers; the relationship depends on which centers differ.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Spectroscopy Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a prospective randomized clinical trial to investigate spectroscopy. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: An IR spectrum shows a broad absorption centered near 3300 cm−1 and a sharp absorption at 1715 cm−1. Which functional groups are most consistent with these peaks?

choices.text: an alcohol O–H (broad 3200–3550 cm−1) and a carbonyl C=O (sharp ~1715 cm−1)
an alkyne C≡C (~2100–2260 cm−1) and an alcohol O–H (~3300 cm−1)
an amine N–H (sharp doublet ~3300–3500 cm−1) and an alkene C=C (~1640 cm−1)
an aldehyde C–H (two weak peaks ~2700–2850 cm−1) and a C–O ether stretch (~1100 cm−1)

explanation.short: Broad O–H: 3200–3550 cm−1 (alcohol) or 2500–3300 cm−1 (carboxylic acid). Carbonyl C=O: ~1715 cm−1 (ketone/acid), ~1735 cm−1 (ester), ~1670 cm−1 (amide). Aldehyde C–H: ~2720 and 2820 cm−1.
explanation.detailed: Broad O–H: 3200–3550 cm−1 (alcohol) or 2500–3300 cm−1 (carboxylic acid). Carbonyl C=O: ~1715 cm−1 (ketone/acid), ~1735 cm−1 (ester), ~1670 cm−1 (amide). Aldehyde C–H: ~2720 and 2820 cm−1. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: A is correct: an alcohol O–H (broad 3200–3550 cm−1) and a carbonyl C=O (sharp ~1715 cm−1).

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Alkyne triple bond absorbs ~2100–2260 cm−1; the 1715 cm−1 carbonyl is inconsistent with this pairing
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Amine N–H appears as a sharp doublet (primary) or singlet (secondary), not a broad single peak; alkene C=C absorbs ~1640 cm−1, not 1715 cm−1
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Aldehyde C–H appears as two weak peaks near 2700–2850 cm−1, not a broad 3300 cm−1 absorption; ether C–O is ~1100 cm−1, not 1715

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Broad O–H ~3300 = alcohol. Carbonyl ~1715 = ketone or acid. Aldehyde: two weak C–H peaks ~2700–2850.
explanation.common_trap: Mistaking the aldehyde C–H doublet for alcohol O–H; aldehyde peak is weak and appears as two peaks, not a broad hump.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Expectation, conditioning, and therapeutic relationship as neurobiologically distinct components of placebo analgesia
passage.text: Expectation, conditioning, and therapeutic relationship as neurobiologically distinct components of placebo analgesia. Background: Whether placebo analgesia is mediated by expectation, conditioning, or patient-provider relationship — and whether these mechanisms are neurobiologically distinct — is unresolved. Methods: Ninety-six healthy participants underwent a within-subject placebo analgesia protocol independently manipulating expectation and conditioning. fMRI was acquired during pain testing; naloxone tested opioid dependence. Results: All three conditions produced significant analgesia.

stem: Which alternative hypothesis would be most difficult to rule out based on the described results?

choices.text: the lack of a negative control means any observed effect could be due to handling alone
the results cannot be generalized because the study used a non-human model system
the study provides evidence that the independent variable produces the observed change in the outcome, consistent with the proposed mechanism described in the abstract
the correlational design proves a direct causal relationship between the variables measured

explanation.short: Research passage questions require identifying what the data support versus what they prove, and distinguishing study limitations from study invalidation.
explanation.detailed: Research passage questions require identifying what the data support versus what they prove, and distinguishing study limitations from study invalidation. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: the study provides evidence that the independent variable produces the observed change in the outcome, consistent with the proposed mechanism described in the abstract.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: The study may have a negative control not explicitly mentioned; this extreme inference goes beyond the information given
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Model systems have limitations but provide mechanistic evidence; failure to generalize is a concern, not an absolute disqualifier
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Even well-designed studies cannot prove causation from correlation; the word 'proves' is too strong and is a classic wrong-answer signal on the MCAT

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Evidence 'supports' a conclusion; it rarely 'proves' one. Always ask: what does the control group tell you?
explanation.common_trap: Selecting answers that use absolute language ('proves,' 'cannot,' 'always') when the data only support a probabilistic conclusion.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Work and Energy Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a retrospective cohort study in hospitalized patients to investigate work and energy. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: A skier descends a frictionless slope, dropping 10 m vertically. Using energy conservation, what is the skier's speed at the bottom (g = 10 m/s²)?

choices.text: 80 J, calculated as W = Fd = 20 × 4, ignoring the angle
approximately 69 J, calculated as W = Fd cos θ = 20 × 4 × cos 30° ≈ 69 J
0 J, because only the horizontal component of velocity matters
40 J, calculated using sin 30° instead of cos 30°

explanation.short: W = Fd cos θ. The force component along the direction of motion is F cos θ. W = 20 × 4 × cos 30° = 80 × 0.866 ≈ 69 J.
explanation.detailed: W = Fd cos θ. The force component along the direction of motion is F cos θ. W = 20 × 4 × cos 30° = 80 × 0.866 ≈ 69 J. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: approximately 69 J, calculated as W = Fd cos θ = 20 × 4 × cos 30° ≈ 69 J.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: W = Fd only when force is parallel to displacement; the angle must be accounted for with cos θ
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Work is force times displacement in the direction of force regardless of velocity; 0 J is only correct when force is perpendicular to displacement
wrong_answer_explanations.D: The component of force along the displacement uses cos θ, not sin θ; sin 30° = 0.5 gives 40 J, which is incorrect

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: W = Fd cos θ. Perpendicular force does zero work. Parallel force does maximal work.
explanation.common_trap: Using the full force magnitude without the cosine factor; always project force onto displacement.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Experimental Passage: Enzyme Inhibition Kinetics
passage.text: Researchers investigated the kinetics of a hepatic enzyme responsible for metabolizing a prodrug to its active form. The enzyme was incubated with varying concentrations of substrate in the presence or absence of a small-molecule inhibitor at a fixed concentration of 50 μM. Reaction velocity was measured by monitoring product formation spectrophotometrically over 5 minutes. Results are shown in Table 1. A Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot was subsequently constructed; the inhibited and control lines intersect on the y-axis, while the x-intercept shifted closer to zero in the presence of the inhibitor.

tables.title: Table 1. Reaction velocity (μmol/min) at varying substrate concentrations

stem: At very high [S] (>> Km), how would the inhibited velocity compare to the control velocity?

choices.text: noncompetitive inhibition, because velocity is reduced at all substrate concentrations tested
competitive inhibition, because the y-intercept (1/Vmax) is unchanged while the x-intercept (−1/Km) shifts, indicating elevated apparent Km without altered Vmax
irreversible inhibition, because substrate excess at 100 mM does not fully restore velocity to the uninhibited value
uncompetitive inhibition, because both Km and Vmax would decrease proportionally, giving parallel Lineweaver-Burk lines

explanation.short: Competitive inhibitors bind the active site reversibly and are displaced by high substrate. This raises apparent Km (inhibitor effectively requires more substrate to compete) without altering Vmax. Lineweaver-Burk: same y-intercept (1/Vmax), shifted x-intercept (−1/Km(app)).
explanation.detailed: Competitive inhibitors bind the active site reversibly and are displaced by high substrate. This raises apparent Km (inhibitor effectively requires more substrate to compete) without altering Vmax. Lineweaver-Burk: same y-intercept (1/Vmax), shifted x-intercept (−1/Km(app)). This item tests integration of clinical findings with underlying physiology.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: competitive inhibition, because the y-intercept (1/Vmax) is unchanged while the x-intercept (−1/Km) shifts, indicating elevated apparent Km without altered Vmax.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Noncompetitive inhibition shifts the y-intercept (changes 1/Vmax) without changing the x-intercept; here the y-intercept is the same for inhibited and control
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: At 100 mM in Table 1 the inhibited velocity (91) approaches the control (95), showing convergence at high [S] — the hallmark of competitive, not irreversible, inhibition
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Uncompetitive inhibition produces parallel Lineweaver-Burk lines (both intercepts shift equally); here only the x-intercept shifts

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: competitive inhibition, because the y-intercept (1/Vmax) is unchanged while the x-intercept (−1/Km) shifts, indicating elevated apparent Km without altered Vmax
explanation.common_trap: Focusing on individual lab values rather than the clinical pattern as a whole.
explanation.how_to_think: Identify the primary disturbance from the lab pattern, then trace the underlying mechanism.

stem: Three resistors of 6 Ω, 3 Ω, and 2 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?

choices.text: 2 Ω, by taking only the smallest resistance
3 Ω, by averaging the three resistances
11 Ω, calculated by summing resistances as if in series

explanation.short: Parallel: 1/Req = Σ(1/Ri). Series: Req = ΣRi. Parallel resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance.
explanation.detailed: Parallel: 1/Req = Σ(1/Ri). Series: Req = ΣRi. Parallel resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: 1 Ω, calculated from 1/Req = 1/6 + 1/3 + 1/2 = 1/6 + 2/6 + 3/6 = 6/6 = 1.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: The equivalent parallel resistance is always less than the smallest branch resistor; taking the minimum directly ignores the other paths
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Averaging has no basis in circuit analysis; the reciprocal formula must be applied
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Adding resistances directly applies to series circuits; parallel resistors always yield a lower equivalent resistance than any single branch

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Parallel: 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …. Result is always lower than smallest branch.
explanation.common_trap: Adding parallel resistors as if in series (the most common error); parallel adds conductances, not resistances.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Fluids Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a series of in vivo NMR spectroscopy experiments to investigate fluids. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: Blood flows through a wide aorta into a narrower artery. According to the continuity equation, how does velocity change?

choices.text: resistance increases by a factor of 16, because Poiseuille resistance is inversely proportional to radius to the fourth power
resistance increases by a factor of 2, because halving the radius doubles the resistance
resistance decreases because a narrower vessel allows faster flow
resistance increases by a factor of 4, because area decreases by a factor of 4 when radius halves

explanation.short: Poiseuille: R = 8ηL/(πr⁴). Halving r increases R by (1/0.5)⁴ = 2⁴ = 16. Small changes in vessel radius have dramatic effects on resistance.
explanation.detailed: Poiseuille: R = 8ηL/(πr⁴). Halving r increases R by (1/0.5)⁴ = 2⁴ = 16. Small changes in vessel radius have dramatic effects on resistance. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: A is correct: resistance increases by a factor of 16, because Poiseuille resistance is inversely proportional to radius to the fourth power.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Resistance scales with r⁻⁴, not r⁻¹; halving r raises resistance by 2⁴ = 16, not 2
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Resistance increases in a narrower vessel; while velocity can increase (continuity), the driving pressure required rises dramatically
wrong_answer_explanations.D: The r⁴ relationship is steeper than proportional to area; a factor of 4 would apply to a simple area-based formula

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Poiseuille: R ∝ 1/r⁴. Halving radius → 16× resistance. Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
explanation.common_trap: Using r² (area) instead of r⁴ in Poiseuille's law; the fourth-power dependence is the high-yield fact here.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

9 m/s
12 m/s
18 m/s

explanation.detailed: v = v₀ + at. Starting from rest (v₀ = 0): v = 0 + at. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: 9 m/s.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This distractor targets a common misconception about the mechanism or relationship.

wrong_answer_explanations.C: This distractor targets a common misconception about the mechanism or relationship.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Apply v = v₀ + at when the problem gives the relevant variables.

passage.title: Optics Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a cell-free translation system to investigate optics. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: A converging lens with focal length 10 cm forms an image of an object placed 30 cm from the lens. Which description of the image is correct?

choices.text: a virtual, upright image located 15 cm from the lens on the same side as the object
no image forms because the object is beyond the focal length
a real, inverted, and diminished image located 15 cm from the lens on the far side
a real, upright image located 30 cm from the lens

explanation.short: 1/f = 1/do + 1/di → 1/10 = 1/30 + 1/di → 1/di = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30 → di = 15 cm. Positive di = real and inverted.
explanation.detailed: 1/f = 1/do + 1/di → 1/10 = 1/30 + 1/di → 1/di = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30 → di = 15 cm. Positive di = real and inverted. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: a real, inverted, and diminished image located 15 cm from the lens on the far side.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Virtual, upright images form only when the object is inside the focal length; here object distance (30 cm) > f (10 cm), so a real image forms
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Objects beyond the focal length always produce real images; objects inside the focal length produce virtual images
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Real images formed by converging lenses are always inverted; a real upright image is impossible with a single converging lens

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Thin lens: 1/f = 1/do + 1/di. Positive di → real, inverted image. Negative di → virtual, upright.
explanation.common_trap: Assuming objects beyond 2f always produce diminished images; use the lens equation to calculate rather than guess.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Waves Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a double-blind crossover design with healthy volunteers to investigate waves. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: Two waves of equal amplitude and frequency interfere. One wave is shifted by half a wavelength relative to the other. What is the resultant amplitude?

choices.text: resonance: the truck's frequency matches the observer's natural frequency
the Doppler effect: the observer perceives higher frequency because successive wave crests arrive more frequently as the source approaches
diffraction: sound bends around the observer causing frequency increase
constructive interference: approaching sources always amplify sound

explanation.short: Doppler effect: when source and observer approach, observed frequency f' = f(v+vo)/(v−vs). Moving source approaching → f' > f; receding → f' < f.
explanation.detailed: Doppler effect: when source and observer approach, observed frequency f' = f(v+vo)/(v−vs). Moving source approaching → f' > f; receding → f' < f. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: the Doppler effect: the observer perceives higher frequency because successive wave crests arrive more frequently as the source approaches.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Resonance requires matching natural frequencies of a resonating body; it does not cause a frequency shift tied to source motion
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Diffraction is bending of waves around obstacles; it does not shift the perceived frequency
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Constructive interference involves overlapping waves in space, not a moving source; the effect disappears when the truck passes

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Doppler: approaching source → higher observed frequency. Receding → lower. Half-wavelength shift → destructive interference (amplitude = 0).
explanation.common_trap: Confusing Doppler (frequency shift from motion) with changes in amplitude or resonance phenomena.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: A researcher cannot directly measure the enthalpy of combustion of carbon to CO because CO₂ forms simultaneously. Which approach allows indirect determination of ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g)?

choices.text: Hess's Law states that enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH for a reaction equals the sum of ΔH values for any series of steps connecting the same reactants and products; reversing a step negates its ΔH.
Enthalpy changes must be measured directly because they depend on the reaction pathway
Hess's Law applies only when all steps occur at the same temperature and pressure
Reversing a reaction step does not change the sign of ΔH, only its magnitude

explanation.short: Hess's Law follows from enthalpy being a state function: ΔH depends only on initial and final states, not on the route taken. To find ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂ → CO, reverse reaction 2 (ΔH = +283.0 kJ) and add it to reaction 1 (ΔH = −393.5 kJ), giving ΔH = −110.5 kJ. Intermediates that appear on both sides cancel.
explanation.detailed: Hess's Law follows from enthalpy being a state function: ΔH depends only on initial and final states, not on the route taken. To find ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂ → CO, reverse reaction 2 (ΔH = +283.0 kJ) and add it to reaction 1 (ΔH = −393.5 kJ), giving ΔH = −110.5 kJ. Intermediates that appear on both sides cancel. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: A is correct: Hess's Law states that enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH for a reaction equals the sum of ΔH values for any series of steps connecting the same reactants and products; reversing a step negates its ΔH..

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Enthalpy is explicitly a state function, meaning it is entirely pathway-independent and can always be summed algebraically
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Hess's Law holds at any constant pressure regardless of temperature because enthalpy is a state function, not pathway-dependent
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Reversing a reaction reverses the direction of heat flow, so ΔH must change sign (e.g., endothermic becomes exothermic)

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Hess's Law: ΔH_rxn = Σ(ΔH steps); reverse a step → flip the sign of ΔH.
explanation.common_trap: Students forget to flip the sign of ΔH when reversing a reaction step, leading to an answer that is off by 2× the reversed step's value.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Clinical Vignette: Acid-Base Disturbance
passage.text: A 24-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department by his roommate, who found him confused and breathing rapidly. He has not taken insulin for three days. On examination, he is tachycardic (HR 118 bpm), hypotensive (BP 92/60 mmHg), and his breathing is deep and labored. His breath has a fruity odor. Laboratory values are shown in Table 1. Serum ketones are markedly elevated. Urinalysis reveals glucosuria and ketonuria.

tables.title: Table 1. Arterial blood gas and serum chemistry

stem: Which anion gap calculation is consistent with the laboratory findings, and what does an elevated anion gap indicate in this patient?

choices.text: respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation caused by hyperventilation from anxiety or pain
normal anion gap metabolic acidosis caused by bicarbonate loss through diarrhea or renal tubular acidosis
high anion gap metabolic acidosis caused by ketoacid accumulation from uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation caused by hypoventilation from altered consciousness

explanation.short: DKA: insulin deficiency → lipolysis → β-oxidation → acetyl-CoA overflow → ketone bodies → high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Kussmaul respirations (deep, labored breathing) lower PaCO₂ as respiratory compensation.
explanation.detailed: DKA: insulin deficiency → lipolysis → β-oxidation → acetyl-CoA overflow → ketone bodies → high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Kussmaul respirations (deep, labored breathing) lower PaCO₂ as respiratory compensation. This item tests integration of clinical findings with underlying physiology.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: high anion gap metabolic acidosis caused by ketoacid accumulation from uncontrolled diabetes mellitus.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Respiratory alkalosis requires elevated pH; Table 1 shows pH 7.22, confirming acidosis, not alkalosis
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Normal anion gap acidosis (AG = Na − Cl − HCO₃ = 138 − 108 − 12 = 18, elevated > 12) does not fit; the increased AG points to unmeasured ketoacids, not bicarbonate loss
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Respiratory acidosis requires elevated PaCO₂; Table 1 shows low PaCO₂ (28 mmHg), indicating hyperventilation rather than hypoventilation

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: high anion gap metabolic acidosis caused by ketoacid accumulation from uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
explanation.common_trap: Focusing on individual lab values rather than the clinical pattern as a whole.
explanation.how_to_think: Identify the primary disturbance from the lab pattern, then trace the underlying mechanism.

passage.title: Specific Heat Capacity Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a controlled murine model with genetic knockout to investigate specific heat capacity. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: Two metals of equal mass are heated with the same amount of energy. Metal A shows a 10 °C rise; Metal B shows a 25 °C rise. Which metal has the higher specific heat capacity?

choices.text: Specific heat capacity (c) relates heat flow to mass and temperature change by q = mcΔT; a substance with a high c requires more energy per gram per degree, making water (c = 4.18 J/g·°C) an exceptional thermal buffer.
q = mΔT only; specific heat capacity is not needed if mass and temperature change are known
Specific heat capacity and heat capacity are interchangeable terms regardless of sample mass
A higher specific heat capacity means a substance heats up faster for the same energy input

explanation.short: The equation q = mcΔT quantifies heat exchange: q in joules, m in grams, c in J/(g·°C), and ΔT = T_final − T_initial. Water's unusually high specific heat (4.18 J/g·°C) arises from extensive hydrogen bonding and is crucial for temperature homeostasis in biological systems. In calorimetry, q_solution = −q_reaction by conservation of energy.
explanation.detailed: The equation q = mcΔT quantifies heat exchange: q in joules, m in grams, c in J/(g·°C), and ΔT = T_final − T_initial. Water's unusually high specific heat (4.18 J/g·°C) arises from extensive hydrogen bonding and is crucial for temperature homeostasis in biological systems. In calorimetry, q_solution = −q_reaction by conservation of energy. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: A is correct: Specific heat capacity (c) relates heat flow to mass and temperature change by q = mcΔT; a substance with a high c requires more energy per gram per degree, making water (c = 4.18 J/g·°C) an exceptional thermal buffer..

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.B: The equation requires all three variables—mass, specific heat capacity, and ΔT—because q = mcΔT, not q = mΔT
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Specific heat capacity (c) is an intensive property (per gram), while heat capacity (C) is extensive (for a given sample); C = mc
wrong_answer_explanations.D: A higher specific heat capacity means a substance heats up more slowly (smaller ΔT) for the same energy input, not faster

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: q = mcΔT; water's high specific heat (4.18 J/g·°C) stabilizes biological temperatures.
explanation.common_trap: Students confuse specific heat capacity (intensive, per gram) with heat capacity (extensive, for whole sample), causing errors when masses differ.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Ideal Gas Laws Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a prospective randomized clinical trial to investigate ideal gas laws. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: A gas sample has P = 2 atm, V = 3 L, and T = 300 K. How many moles of gas are present? (R = 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K)

choices.text: Charles's Law states that volume is inversely proportional to temperature at constant pressure
Boyle's Law states that volume is directly proportional to pressure at constant temperature
The ideal gas law applies accurately to all gases under all conditions of pressure and temperature

The ideal gas law PV = nRT unifies Boyle's Law (PV = constant at fixed T,n) and Charles's Law (V/T = constant at fixed P,n); for the MCAT, recognize that doubling T at constant P doubles V, and halving V at constant T doubles P.

explanation.short: PV = nRT is the cornerstone ideal gas relationship. Boyle's Law (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ at constant T) and Charles's Law (V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ at constant P) are special cases. Temperature must always be in Kelvin. For the syringe problem: V₂ = (1 atm × 60 mL)/3 atm = 20 mL. For moles: n = PV/RT = (2 × 3)/(0.0821 × 300) ≈ 0.24 mol.
explanation.detailed: PV = nRT is the cornerstone ideal gas relationship. Boyle's Law (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ at constant T) and Charles's Law (V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ at constant P) are special cases. Temperature must always be in Kelvin. For the syringe problem: V₂ = (1 atm × 60 mL)/3 atm = 20 mL. For moles: n = PV/RT = (2 × 3)/(0.0821 × 300) ≈ 0.24 mol. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: The ideal gas law PV = nRT unifies Boyle's Law (PV = constant at fixed T,n) and Charles's Law (V/T = constant at fixed P,n); for the MCAT, recognize that doubling T at constant P doubles V, and halving V at constant T doubles P..

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Charles's Law states volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature (V/T = k), so increasing temperature increases volume
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Boyle's Law states volume is inversely proportional to pressure (PV = k), so increasing pressure decreases volume
wrong_answer_explanations.C: The ideal gas law is an approximation that fails at high pressures and low temperatures where intermolecular forces and finite molecular volume become significant
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: PV = nRT; always use Kelvin; Boyle's: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂; Charles's: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.
explanation.common_trap: Students use Celsius instead of Kelvin in gas law calculations, producing dramatically wrong answers, especially near 0 °C.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Real Gases and Van der Waals Equation Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a retrospective cohort study in hospitalized patients to investigate real gases and van der waals equation. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: At high pressure and low temperature, a real gas deviates significantly from ideal behavior. Which factor causes the measured volume to be larger than predicted by the ideal gas law?

choices.text: Real gases deviate from ideal behavior only at low pressures where molecules are far apart

The van der Waals equation corrects for two non-ideal behaviors: the 'a' term (a/V²) accounts for attractive intermolecular forces that reduce effective pressure, while the 'b' term accounts for the finite volume of gas molecules that reduces available free volume.
The 'a' correction in van der Waals accounts for the finite size (volume) of gas molecules
The 'b' correction accounts for intermolecular attractions that reduce the observed pressure

explanation.short: Ideal gas law assumes point-mass molecules with no intermolecular forces. Real gases deviate: at high P, molecular volume (b term) causes V_real > V_ideal; at low T, attractions (a term) cause P_real < P_ideal. NH₃ deviates more than Ne because NH₃ has strong hydrogen bonding (large a) and larger molecular volume (large b), while Ne is a small noble gas with only weak London dispersion forces.
explanation.detailed: Ideal gas law assumes point-mass molecules with no intermolecular forces. Real gases deviate: at high P, molecular volume (b term) causes V_real > V_ideal; at low T, attractions (a term) cause P_real < P_ideal. NH₃ deviates more than Ne because NH₃ has strong hydrogen bonding (large a) and larger molecular volume (large b), while Ne is a small noble gas with only weak London dispersion forces. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: The van der Waals equation corrects for two non-ideal behaviors: the 'a' term (a/V²) accounts for attractive intermolecular forces that reduce effective pressure, while the 'b' term accounts for the finite volume of gas molecules that reduces available free volume..

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Real gases deviate most at high pressures (molecules are close, volume matters) and low temperatures (molecules move slowly, attractions matter more)
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: The 'a' correction accounts for intermolecular attractions (not molecular size); 'b' accounts for finite molecular volume
wrong_answer_explanations.D: The 'b' correction accounts for the excluded volume of molecules themselves, not for intermolecular attractions

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Van der Waals: 'a' corrects for attractions (reduces P), 'b' corrects for molecular volume (reduces V); polar/large molecules deviate most.
explanation.common_trap: Students mix up which correction term (a vs b) corresponds to which physical property—attractions vs molecular size.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Impaired PI3K-Akt signaling reduces GLUT4 vesicle translocation to the plasma membrane in skeletal muscle of type 2 diabetic subjects
passage.text: Impaired PI3K-Akt signaling reduces GLUT4 vesicle translocation to the plasma membrane in skeletal muscle of type 2 diabetic subjects. Background: Insulin resistance in skeletal muscle is a hallmark of type 2 diabetes. Insulin normally promotes GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane via PI3K-Akt-AS160 signaling. Methods: Muscle biopsies from 18 T2DM patients and 18 controls were obtained before and after euglycemic-hyperinsulinemic clamp; PI3K activity, Akt phosphorylation, AS160 phosphorylation, and GLUT4 surface density were quantified.

stem: Which modification to the experimental design would best address a potential confound in this study?

choices.text: the lack of a negative control means any observed effect could be due to handling alone
the results cannot be generalized because the study used a non-human model system
the study provides evidence that the independent variable produces the observed change in the outcome, consistent with the proposed mechanism described in the abstract
the correlational design proves a direct causal relationship between the variables measured

explanation.short: Research passage questions require identifying what the data support versus what they prove, and distinguishing study limitations from study invalidation.
explanation.detailed: Research passage questions require identifying what the data support versus what they prove, and distinguishing study limitations from study invalidation. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: the study provides evidence that the independent variable produces the observed change in the outcome, consistent with the proposed mechanism described in the abstract.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: The study may have a negative control not explicitly mentioned; this extreme inference goes beyond the information given
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Model systems have limitations but provide mechanistic evidence; failure to generalize is a concern, not an absolute disqualifier
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Even well-designed studies cannot prove causation from correlation; the word 'proves' is too strong and is a classic wrong-answer signal on the MCAT

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Evidence 'supports' a conclusion; it rarely 'proves' one. Always ask: what does the control group tell you?
explanation.common_trap: Selecting answers that use absolute language ('proves,' 'cannot,' 'always') when the data only support a probabilistic conclusion.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

stem: For CaF₂ (Ksp = 3.9 × 10⁻¹¹), what is the molar solubility in pure water compared to in 0.10 M NaF solution?

choices.text: The common-ion effect reduces the solubility of a slightly soluble salt when a soluble salt sharing a common ion is added; the added ion shifts the equilibrium toward precipitation, decreasing solubility as predicted by Le Chatelier's principle.
When Q > Ksp, the solution is unsaturated and no precipitation occurs
Adding a common ion increases solubility by providing more ions to stabilize the crystal lattice
Ksp changes when a common ion is added because the ionic strength of the solution changes

explanation.short: Ksp is the solubility product constant for dissolution equilibrium: CaF₂ ⇌ Ca²⁺ + 2F⁻, Ksp = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]². In pure water, s = (Ksp/4)^(1/3) ≈ 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ M. In 0.10 M NaF, [F⁻] ≈ 0.10 M, so s = Ksp/(0.10)² = 3.9 × 10⁻⁹ M—about 50,000× less soluble. This is the common-ion effect: a shared ion suppresses dissolution.
explanation.detailed: Ksp is the solubility product constant for dissolution equilibrium: CaF₂ ⇌ Ca²⁺ + 2F⁻, Ksp = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]². In pure water, s = (Ksp/4)^(1/3) ≈ 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ M. In 0.10 M NaF, [F⁻] ≈ 0.10 M, so s = Ksp/(0.10)² = 3.9 × 10⁻⁹ M—about 50,000× less soluble. This is the common-ion effect: a shared ion suppresses dissolution. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: A is correct: The common-ion effect reduces the solubility of a slightly soluble salt when a soluble salt sharing a common ion is added; the added ion shifts the equilibrium toward precipitation, decreasing solubility as predicted by Le Chatelier's principle..

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.B: When Q > Ksp, the solution is supersaturated and precipitation occurs until Q = Ksp
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Adding a common ion decreases solubility by shifting equilibrium toward the solid precipitate per Le Chatelier's principle
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Ksp is a constant at a given temperature and does not change with added ions; only solubility (the amount dissolved) changes

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: Common-ion effect: adding a shared ion suppresses solubility; Ksp stays constant but molar solubility decreases dramatically.
explanation.common_trap: Students confuse Ksp (which is constant at fixed T) with molar solubility (which changes with common ions), claiming Ksp 'decreases' when a common ion is added.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Clinical Vignette: Chronic Kidney Disease
passage.text: A 68-year-old woman with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents for follow-up. She reports progressive fatigue, decreased urine output, and bilateral leg swelling over the past month. Medications include lisinopril, metformin, and amlodipine. Blood pressure is 158/96 mmHg; she has 2+ pitting edema to the knees. Laboratory values are shown in Table 1. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein. Renal ultrasound reveals bilaterally small, echogenic kidneys.

stem: Based on Table 1, which mechanism best explains the elevated serum potassium in this patient?

choices.text: elevated potassium results from transcellular shifts caused by metabolic alkalosis shifting K⁺ into cells
reduced GFR from chronic diabetic nephropathy impairs potassium secretion in the cortical collecting duct, leading to hyperkalemia
hyperkalemia is caused by ACE inhibitor use alone, independent of any reduction in GFR
hyperkalemia results from decreased filtered potassium load, preventing renal potassium excretion

explanation.short: In CKD, fewer functional nephrons means reduced aldosterone-responsive collecting duct capacity for K⁺ secretion. Concurrent metabolic acidosis (from impaired H⁺ excretion) shifts K⁺ out of cells, further raising plasma levels.
explanation.detailed: In CKD, fewer functional nephrons means reduced aldosterone-responsive collecting duct capacity for K⁺ secretion. Concurrent metabolic acidosis (from impaired H⁺ excretion) shifts K⁺ out of cells, further raising plasma levels. This item tests integration of clinical findings with underlying physiology.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: reduced GFR from chronic diabetic nephropathy impairs potassium secretion in the cortical collecting duct, leading to hyperkalemia.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: This patient has metabolic acidosis (HCO₃⁻ 14 mEq/L), which shifts K⁺ out of cells (raising plasma K⁺); alkalosis would shift it in; the primary cause is reduced tubular secretion
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: While ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone-mediated K⁺ secretion, the primary driver here is CKD reducing functional nephron mass and tubular secretory capacity overall
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Potassium excretion is driven primarily by secretion in the collecting duct, not filtered load; GFR reduction impairs secretory capacity in remaining nephrons

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: reduced GFR from chronic diabetic nephropathy impairs potassium secretion in the cortical collecting duct, leading to hyperkalemia
explanation.common_trap: Focusing on individual lab values rather than the clinical pattern as a whole.
explanation.how_to_think: Identify the primary disturbance from the lab pattern, then trace the underlying mechanism.

passage.title: Kw and Water Autoionization Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a series of in vivo NMR spectroscopy experiments to investigate kw and water autoionization. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: Why does the pH of neutral water decrease as temperature increases, even though the solution remains neutral?

choices.text: As temperature rises, water becomes acidic because more H⁺ ions are produced than OH⁻ ions
At 37 °C, neutral pH is still 7.0 because neutrality is defined as pH 7 regardless of temperature

Water autoionizes according to 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ with Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C; at 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14, and a neutral solution has pH = pOH = 7, but Kw increases with temperature so neutral pH < 7 at elevated temperatures.
pOH = 14 − pH at all temperatures because Kw is always 10⁻¹⁴

explanation.short: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C; taking −log of both sides gives pH + pOH = pKw = 14. If [OH⁻] = 10⁻³ M, pOH = 3, pH = 11. At 37 °C, Kw = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ so pKw = 13.62; neutral pH = 6.81, not 7.0. Neutrality means [H⁺] = [OH⁻], not pH = 7.
explanation.detailed: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C; taking −log of both sides gives pH + pOH = pKw = 14. If [OH⁻] = 10⁻³ M, pOH = 3, pH = 11. At 37 °C, Kw = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ so pKw = 13.62; neutral pH = 6.81, not 7.0. Neutrality means [H⁺] = [OH⁻], not pH = 7. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: C is correct: Water autoionizes according to 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ with Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C; at 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14, and a neutral solution has pH = pOH = 7, but Kw increases with temperature so neutral pH < 7 at elevated temperatures..

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Water's autoionization is endothermic, so higher T increases both [H⁺] and [OH⁻] equally; the solution remains neutral (equal concentrations) but pH falls because pKw decreases
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Neutral pH is defined as pH = pOH (equal [H⁺] and [OH⁻]), not as pH = 7; at 37 °C, neutral pH = ½ × pKw = ½ × 13.62 ≈ 6.81
wrong_answer_explanations.C: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.D: pOH = pKw − pH, and pKw only equals 14 at 25 °C; at higher temperatures pKw decreases, so pH + pOH < 14

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: pH + pOH = pKw = 14 at 25 °C; neutral means [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so neutral pH = 7 only at 25 °C.
explanation.common_trap: Students assume neutral pH = 7 at all temperatures; at body temperature, neutral pH is closer to 6.8.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Alpha Decay Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a cell-free translation system to investigate alpha decay. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: Radon-222 undergoes alpha decay in homes and is a leading cause of lung cancer. What daughter nucleus is produced when ²²²Rn undergoes alpha decay?

choices.text: Alpha decay decreases the atomic number by 1 and mass number by 2, equivalent to emitting a deuterium nucleus
Alpha particles penetrate most materials easily due to their high kinetic energy
Alpha decay does not change the element because the nuclear charge is preserved by emitting equal numbers of protons and neutrons

In alpha (α) decay, the nucleus emits a ⁴He nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons), decreasing the parent's atomic number by 2 and mass number by 4, producing a daughter nuclide two elements to the left on the periodic table.

explanation.short: An alpha particle (⁴He, Z=2, A=4) is emitted: Z_daughter = Z_parent − 2; A_daughter = A_parent − 4. For ²³⁸U (Z=92): daughter is ²³⁴Th (Z=90). For ²²²Rn (Z=86): daughter is ²¹⁸Po (Z=84). Despite low penetrating power, inhaled alpha emitters cause severe local tissue damage because all ionizing energy is deposited in a tiny volume.
explanation.detailed: An alpha particle (⁴He, Z=2, A=4) is emitted: Z_daughter = Z_parent − 2; A_daughter = A_parent − 4. For ²³⁸U (Z=92): daughter is ²³⁴Th (Z=90). For ²²²Rn (Z=86): daughter is ²¹⁸Po (Z=84). Despite low penetrating power, inhaled alpha emitters cause severe local tissue damage because all ionizing energy is deposited in a tiny volume. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: In alpha (α) decay, the nucleus emits a ⁴He nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons), decreasing the parent's atomic number by 2 and mass number by 4, producing a daughter nuclide two elements to the left on the periodic table..

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Alpha decay decreases atomic number by 2 and mass number by 4 (a ⁴He nucleus), not by 1 and 2
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Alpha particles are heavily ionizing but have very short range in matter (~5 cm in air) and are stopped by paper or skin due to their large mass and charge (+2)
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Alpha decay ejects 2 protons, reducing atomic number by 2 and changing the element to one two positions left in the periodic table
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: α decay: atomic number −2, mass number −4; daughter is two elements left on periodic table.
explanation.common_trap: Students subtract 2 from the mass number instead of 4 when predicting the daughter nuclide.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Beta Decay and Gamma Emission Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a double-blind crossover design with healthy volunteers to investigate beta decay and gamma emission. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: ¹³¹I is used in thyroid cancer treatment and undergoes β⁻ decay followed by γ emission. Why does γ emission not change the nuclide's atomic or mass number?

choices.text: In β⁺ decay, a neutron converts to a proton, so the atomic number increases by 1

In β⁻ decay, a neutron converts to a proton plus an electron (β⁻ particle) and an antineutrino, increasing atomic number by 1 with no change in mass number; γ emission releases excess nuclear energy as a high-energy photon without changing atomic or mass number.
Beta decay decreases the mass number by 1 because an electron is lost from the nucleus
Gamma emission increases the atomic number by 1 because of the high-energy photon released

explanation.short: β⁻ decay: n → p⁺ + e⁻ + ν̄; atomic number increases by 1, mass number unchanged. ¹⁴C (Z=6) → ¹⁴N (Z=7). β⁺ decay: p → n + e⁺ + ν; atomic number decreases by 1. γ emission releases only energy (E = hf) from an excited nucleus, changing neither Z nor A. All three types are used clinically: ¹³¹I delivers β⁻ and γ radiation to thyroid tissue.
explanation.detailed: β⁻ decay: n → p⁺ + e⁻ + ν̄; atomic number increases by 1, mass number unchanged. ¹⁴C (Z=6) → ¹⁴N (Z=7). β⁺ decay: p → n + e⁺ + ν; atomic number decreases by 1. γ emission releases only energy (E = hf) from an excited nucleus, changing neither Z nor A. All three types are used clinically: ¹³¹I delivers β⁻ and γ radiation to thyroid tissue. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: In β⁻ decay, a neutron converts to a proton plus an electron (β⁻ particle) and an antineutrino, increasing atomic number by 1 with no change in mass number; γ emission releases excess nuclear energy as a high-energy photon without changing atomic or mass number..

wrong_answer_explanations.A: In β⁺ decay, a proton converts to a neutron, so the atomic number decreases by 1 (not increases); for ¹⁴C β⁻ decay, Z increases from 6 to 7, giving ¹⁴N
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Beta particles are electrons ejected from the nucleus but not from orbital electrons; mass number does not change because mass is conserved in the neutron→proton conversion
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Gamma emission is a pure energy release with no change in mass or charge; it lowers the nucleus from an excited state to the ground state

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: β⁻: Z+1, A unchanged; β⁺: Z−1, A unchanged; γ: neither Z nor A changes.
explanation.common_trap: Students think beta particles come from orbital electrons and therefore assume they affect electron configuration rather than nuclear composition.

stem: Which mathematical relationship correctly describes radioactive decay, and why is it called 'first-order' kinetics?

choices.text: The half-life of a radioactive isotope increases as the sample decays because fewer nuclei are available
After 24 days with t₁/₂ = 8 days, the activity of ¹³¹I drops to 25% of the original because 3 half-lives have passed
Radioactive decay is zero-order, so the same number of nuclei decay per unit time regardless of how many remain

Radioactive decay follows first-order kinetics: N(t) = N₀(½)^(t/t₁/₂) or N(t) = N₀e^(−λt) where λ = 0.693/t₁/₂; after each half-life, exactly half the remaining nuclei decay, making the rate proportional to the current number of nuclei.

explanation.short: First-order decay: N(t) = N₀(½)^(t/t₁/₂). For ¹³¹I after 24 days: 24/8 = 3 half-lives; N = 1200 × (½)³ = 150 MBq. For ¹⁴C at 25% remaining: (½)² = 0.25, so 2 half-lives = 2 × 5730 = 11,460 years. The decay constant λ = ln2/t₁/₂ ≈ 0.693/t₁/₂ relates to the probability of decay per unit time.
explanation.detailed: First-order decay: N(t) = N₀(½)^(t/t₁/₂). For ¹³¹I after 24 days: 24/8 = 3 half-lives; N = 1200 × (½)³ = 150 MBq. For ¹⁴C at 25% remaining: (½)² = 0.25, so 2 half-lives = 2 × 5730 = 11,460 years. The decay constant λ = ln2/t₁/₂ ≈ 0.693/t₁/₂ relates to the probability of decay per unit time. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: Radioactive decay follows first-order kinetics: N(t) = N₀(½)^(t/t₁/₂) or N(t) = N₀e^(−λt) where λ = 0.693/t₁/₂; after each half-life, exactly half the remaining nuclei decay, making the rate proportional to the current number of nuclei..

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Half-life is a constant property of a given isotope that does not change with sample size, age, or the amount remaining
wrong_answer_explanations.B: After 3 half-lives (24 days), activity = 1200 × (½)³ = 1200/8 = 150 MBq, not 25%—25% would be after 2 half-lives
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Radioactive decay is first-order: rate = λN, meaning the rate is proportional to N, not constant; as N decreases, the rate of decay also decreases
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: N(t) = N₀(½)^(t/t₁/₂); each half-life halves the remaining activity; t₁/₂ = 0.693/λ.
explanation.common_trap: Students apply half-life linearly (e.g., claiming activity is zero after enough half-lives) rather than exponentially—the quantity asymptotically approaches zero.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.text: Sleep spindles during NREM slow-wave sleep facilitate hippocampal-to-neocortical memory transfer: evidence from targeted memory reactivation. Background: Systems consolidation theory proposes that declarative memories are transferred from hippocampus to neocortex during sleep, but the role of NREM spindles is incompletely understood. Methods: Forty-four adults learned spatial object-location pairs; targeted memory reactivation (TMR) using associated olfactory cues was applied during polysomnographically confirmed NREM sleep. fMRI and EEG were acquired the following morning. Results: TMR items showed 23% higher recall (p<0.001).

the correlational design proves a direct causal relationship between the variables measured

the results cannot be generalized because the study used a non-human model system

passage.title: Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis Scenario
passage.text: Researchers used a controlled murine model with genetic knockout to investigate faraday's laws of electrolysis. Findings are summarized in the data below.

stem: An electrolytic cell deposits copper metal at the cathode. If a current of 2.0 A flows for 96,500 seconds and Cu²⁺ is reduced, how many moles of Cu are deposited?

choices.text: One Faraday of charge (96,485 C) always deposits exactly one mole of any metal, regardless of the ion's charge
Silver and copper cells in series would deposit equal moles of each metal because the same current passes through both
The mass deposited in electrolysis depends on the voltage applied, not on the total charge transferred

Faraday's first law states that the mass of substance deposited is proportional to the total charge passed (Q = It); Faraday's second law states that equivalent quantities of different substances are deposited by the same charge, where 1 mole of electrons (1 Faraday = 96,485 C) deposits 1/n moles of an ion with charge n.

explanation.short: Faraday's laws: moles deposited = Q/(nF) = It/(nF), where n = charge on the ion and F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻. For Cu²⁺ with 2.0 A for 96,500 s: Q = 193,000 C; moles Cu = 193,000/(2 × 96,485) ≈ 1.0 mol. For 0.5 mol Na (n=1): Q = 0.5 × 96,485 ≈ 48,243 C. Ag (n=1) deposits twice the moles of Cu (n=2) for the same charge.
explanation.detailed: Faraday's laws: moles deposited = Q/(nF) = It/(nF), where n = charge on the ion and F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻. For Cu²⁺ with 2.0 A for 96,500 s: Q = 193,000 C; moles Cu = 193,000/(2 × 96,485) ≈ 1.0 mol. For 0.5 mol Na (n=1): Q = 0.5 × 96,485 ≈ 48,243 C. Ag (n=1) deposits twice the moles of Cu (n=2) for the same charge. This item tests MCAT-style mechanistic reasoning.
explanation.why_correct: D is correct: Faraday's first law states that the mass of substance deposited is proportional to the total charge passed (Q = It); Faraday's second law states that equivalent quantities of different substances are deposited by the same charge, where 1 mole of electrons (1 Faraday = 96,485 C) deposits 1/n moles of an ion with charge n..

wrong_answer_explanations.A: One Faraday deposits 1/n moles of a metal whose ion has charge n; Cu²⁺ requires 2 F per mole, Ag⁺ requires only 1 F per mole
wrong_answer_explanations.B: Series cells carry the same charge, but Ag⁺ needs 1 electron per atom while Cu²⁺ needs 2; thus twice as many moles of Ag deposit compared to Cu for the same charge
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Faraday's laws explicitly relate deposited mass to charge (Q = It), not voltage; voltage determines whether electrolysis occurs but not how much product forms
wrong_answer_explanations.D: This is the correct answer.

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: moles deposited = It/(nF); 1 Faraday = 96,485 C deposits 1/n mol of an ion with charge n.
explanation.common_trap: Students forget to divide by n (the ionic charge), depositing twice as many moles as correct for divalent ions like Cu²⁺.
explanation.how_to_think: Predict the expected relationship before reading choices, then eliminate those that reverse or overstate it.

passage.title: Clinical Vignette: Adrenal Cortex Pathology
passage.text: A 34-year-old woman presents with a six-month history of fatigue, weight loss, nausea, and salt craving. Physical examination reveals hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa, skin folds, and elbows. Blood pressure is 88/56 mmHg supine and drops further on standing. Laboratory values are shown in Table 1. A cosyntropin stimulation test fails to produce an appropriate cortisol rise.

stem: The hyperpigmentation in this patient results from which molecular mechanism?

choices.text: tertiary adrenal insufficiency from hypothalamic CRH deficiency, which would reduce both ACTH and cortisol without mineralocorticoid loss

primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease): destruction of the adrenal cortex eliminates both cortisol and aldosterone, removing cortisol's negative feedback on the pituitary and causing compensatory ACTH elevation
secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary failure, which would cause low ACTH and low cortisol without aldosterone deficiency or hyperpigmentation
Cushing's syndrome with adrenal hyperplasia, which causes cortisol excess and would suppress ACTH in most primary adrenal forms

explanation.short: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's): autoimmune destruction of all three cortical zones → absent cortisol (removes negative feedback → ↑ACTH) and absent aldosterone (→ Na⁺ wasting, K⁺ retention, hypotension). High ACTH cross-reacts with melanocortin-1 receptors in skin → hyperpigmentation.
explanation.detailed: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's): autoimmune destruction of all three cortical zones → absent cortisol (removes negative feedback → ↑ACTH) and absent aldosterone (→ Na⁺ wasting, K⁺ retention, hypotension). High ACTH cross-reacts with melanocortin-1 receptors in skin → hyperpigmentation. This item tests integration of clinical findings with underlying physiology.
explanation.why_correct: B is correct: primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease): destruction of the adrenal cortex eliminates both cortisol and aldosterone, removing cortisol's negative feedback on the pituitary and causing compensatory ACTH elevation.

wrong_answer_explanations.A: Tertiary insufficiency: low CRH → low ACTH → low cortisol; ACTH would be low, not elevated as shown; mineralocorticoids remain intact
wrong_answer_explanations.B: This is the correct answer.
wrong_answer_explanations.C: Secondary insufficiency: the pituitary fails → ACTH is low (not high); aldosterone is relatively preserved because it is regulated by RAAS rather than ACTH
wrong_answer_explanations.D: Cushing's syndrome presents with cortisol excess, not deficiency; the patient's low cortisol and high ACTH pattern is opposite to Cushing's

explanation.high_yield_takeaway: primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease): destruction of the adrenal cortex eliminates both cortisol and aldosterone, removing cortisol's negative feedback on the pituitary and causing compensatory ACTH elevation
explanation.common_trap: Focusing on individual lab values rather than the clinical pattern as a whole.
explanation.how_to_think: Identify the primary disturbance from the lab pattern, then trace the underlying mechanism.
